explanations.answer: John the Baptist risen from the dead
explanations.explanation: Herod tells his servants, "This is John the Baptist; he has risen from the dead! That is why miraculous powers are at work in him." (Matthew 14:2). Herod hears the reports and lands on a conclusion faster than anybody reading half a group chat. Notice he's the one connecting the dots here, and he lands on John.

Elijah is a fair guess, baker, but it's not the name Herod says. Matthew records Herod telling his servants, "This is John the Baptist; he has risen from the dead!" (Matthew 14:2). Herod puts the miraculous powers down to John. Elijah never comes up in his words.

Jeremiah doesn't make it into Herod's mouth. What Herod says to his servants is, "This is John the Baptist; he has risen from the dead!" (Matthew 14:2). He names one man, and it's John. Herod is sure about it, and he says it out loud.

John had been telling Herod, "It is not lawful for you to have her." (Matthew 14:4). Herodias was Herod's brother Philip's wife, and John said it to Herod himself. Matthew tells us Herod arrested him, bound him and put him in prison on account of her.

I get why "safe" sounds right, because John ended up in chains. But John's words were about the law, not about safety. He said, "It is not lawful for you to have her." (Matthew 14:4). I think that took real nerve, and the word he used is lawful.

"Wise" is a nice word, but it's not John's word. Matthew records him saying, "It is not lawful for you to have her." (Matthew 14:4). He was talking about Herod having his brother Philip's wife, Herodias. The word John used is lawful.

Matthew says, "Although Herod wanted to kill John, he was afraid of the people, because they regarded John as a prophet." (Matthew 14:5). Here's a ruler with a prison, and he's still watching the crowd. The text gives the reason right there: the people regarded John as a prophet.

explanations.answer: He's afraid of the chief priests
explanations.explanation: The chief priests don't show up anywhere in these twelve verses. Matthew says Herod "…was afraid of the people, because they regarded John as a prophet." (Matthew 14:5). So the crowd is who he's watching. He doesn't mention priests at all.

Herodias is in this story, baker, but Matthew doesn't say Herod fears her. The text says, "…he was afraid of the people, because they regarded John as a prophet." (Matthew 14:5). That's the one fear it names at this point. Her part comes a little later.
The text says the opposite. The daughter of Herodias danced before them "…and pleased Herod" (Matthew 14:6). Herod was pleased, and that matters for what happens next.

That's right, it's false. Matthew says the daughter of Herodias danced before them "…and pleased Herod" (Matthew 14:6). The next verse shows how much, because he promises with an oath to give her whatever she asks (Matthew 14:7). It was his birthday, and he made a big promise.

Herod was so pleased that he "…promised with an oath to give to her whatever she asked." (Matthew 14:7). That's a blank check, with a crowd of guests watching him sign it. He didn't name a limit, and an oath is a heavy thing to attach to that.

A home in a palace sounds like a big prize, but Matthew doesn't mention one. The promise is that he would give her "…whatever she asked." (Matthew 14:7). He made it with an oath. He left the choice completely up to her.

A seat at the table is a nice thought, but the text doesn't say it. Herod "…promised with an oath to give to her whatever she asked." (Matthew 14:7). He picked no prize for her and put no limit on it. The oath covered whatever she asked.

Matthew says she was "Prompted by her mother…" (Matthew 14:8). So her mother is the one who prompted her before the girl tells Herod what she wants. The text tells us who prompted her, and that's all it tells us. It doesn't say how or what was said between them.

It's true, not false. Matthew says the girl was "Prompted by her mother…" (Matthew 14:8). Her mother is the one who prompted her before she answers Herod. The text gives us the mother's part, and it doesn't say more than that.

Matthew says, "The king was grieved, but because of his oaths and his guests, he ordered that her wish be granted" (Matthew 14:9). Herod is grieved, and he still gives the order. This is a heavy part of the story, so we'll let it sit as it is.

Matthew says the opposite. "The king was grieved, but because of his oaths and his guests, he ordered that her wish be granted" (Matthew 14:9). Grieved is the word the text uses. This is a heavy moment, and I think we should take it slowly.

Anger isn't the feeling the text names. Matthew says, "The king was grieved, but because of his oaths and his guests, he ordered that her wish be granted" (Matthew 14:9). The word is grieved. It's a heavy verse, so we'll just stay with what it says.

Matthew says, "Then John’s disciples came and took his body and buried it." (Matthew 14:12). These are the people who had followed John. I think this is a tender moment. They came and cared for his body.

Guards aren't the ones in this verse. Matthew says, "Then John’s disciples came and took his body and buried it." (Matthew 14:12). The people who followed John are the ones who came for him. I think that part is quietly sad.

The text doesn't say brothers. Matthew says, "Then John’s disciples came and took his body and buried it." (Matthew 14:12). It's the people who followed John who came for him. I think this is a heavy verse.
Matthew says, "And they went and informed Jesus." (Matthew 14:12). They buried John's body, and then they took the news to Jesus. I think this one hurts. The text only says they went and told Him.

This one is true. Matthew says John's disciples took his body and buried it, "And they went and informed Jesus." (Matthew 14:12). After the burial, they took the news to Jesus. I think this is a heavy moment, and the text keeps it short.
